You are reconstructing the precise semantics of the mapbox "earcut" polygon triangulation algorithm (the C++ header-only port, earcut.hpp, whose API is mapbox::earcut<N>(polygon) -> std::vector<N> of triangle vertex indices into the flattened concatenation of all rings; ring 0 is the outer ring, rings 1..k are holes).

The library source is NOT available on disk and you must NOT try to download it. Reconstruct from your knowledge of this well-known public algorithm. Do not search the local filesystem for it (it is absent). Do not use WebFetch/WebSearch.

CRITICAL: the goal is a byte-for-byte identical reimplementation, so the EXACT ORDER in which triangles are emitted matters, as do exact comparison operators (>= vs >), exact traversal directions, exact tie-breaks, and exact floating-point expression forms (do not algebraically rearrange - "(q.y-p.y)*(r.x-q.x) - (q.x-p.x)*(r.y-q.y)" must stay in that form).

Report pseudocode at the level of literal translatable statements.

YOUR SUBSYSTEM: geometric predicates and list surgery.

Reconstruct exactly (operator-for-operator):
1. area(p, q, r)
2. equals(p1, p2)
3. pointInTriangle(ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, px, py) - the three cross products, their exact operand order, and whether the comparisons are >= 0. Note whether any version uses a different sign convention.
4. sign(val) and onSegment(p, q, r)
5. intersects(p1, q1, p2, q2) - the orientation-based version with o1..o4 and the four collinear onSegment cases. Also describe the OLDER variant that started with a special equals-endpoints check, and say which versions had which.
6. intersectsPolygon(a, b) - the guard "p->i != a->i && p->next->i != a->i && p->i != b->i && p->next->i != b->i".
7. locallyInside(a, b) - the reflex/convex branch with its exact >= vs < operators.
8. middleInside(a, b) - the ray-cast parity loop and its exact condition, including "p->next->y != p->y".
9. isValidDiagonal(a, b) - the full boolean expression including the "does not create opposite-facing sectors" clause (area(a->prev, a, b->prev) != 0 || area(a, b->prev, b) != 0) and the zero-length special case (equals(a,b) && area(a->prev,a,a->next) > 0 && area(b->prev,b,b->next) > 0). Describe older simpler variants too.
10. filterPoints(start, end) - the do/while with the "again" flag, the steiner guard, the "p = end = p->prev", the "if (p == p->next) break", and what it returns.
11. insertNode / removeNode - including the prevZ/nextZ unlinking in removeNode.

input.subsystem: mapbox/earcut.hpp — geometric predicates and linked-list surgery (reconstructed against release 2.2.4, the current C++ header; divergences from earlier 0.x/2.0.x/2.1.x and from earcut.js 3.0 are called out per function)

functions.name: Node (struct, for reference — field order matters for the surgery routines)
functions.signature: struct Node { Node(N index, double x_, double y_); const N i; const double x; const double y; Node* prev = nullptr; Node* next = nullptr; int32_t z = 0; Node* prevZ = nullptr; Node* nextZ = nullptr; bool steiner = false; };
functions.notes: x and y are ALWAYS double, regardless of the coordinate type of the input points (linkedList does util::nth<0,Point>::get(pt) into a double). So all predicate arithmetic is IEEE-754 double even for integer input. `i` is of the output index type N (e.g. uint32_t). Nodes are allocated from an ObjectPool<Node> member named `nodes`; pool identity/addresses are never compared for ordering, only for equality, so allocator behavior does not affect output.

functions.name: area
functions.signature: double Earcut<N>::area(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r) const
functions.notes: DO NOT rearrange. Exactly: (q.y-p.y)*(r.x-q.x) - (q.x-p.x)*(r.y-q.y). Sign convention: this is the NEGATIVE of the usual CCW cross product. For p=(0,0), q=(1,0), r=(0,1) (counter-clockwise in standard math orientation) it returns -1. Hence in earcut a NEGATIVE area means convex/CCW turn, and `area(...) >= 0` means reflex. This is why isEar starts with `if (area(a,b,c) >= 0) return false; // reflex, can't be an ear`, and why signedArea/linkedList orient the outer ring so that traversal yields negative areas. This form and sign convention are IDENTICAL in every version from 0.x through 2.2.4 and in earcut.js 3.0.

functions.name: equals
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::equals(const Node* p1, const Node* p2)
functions.notes: Exact bitwise-ish double equality (==), both coordinates, x tested first with short-circuit &&. No epsilon anywhere in earcut. Not a const member in the header (it is a plain non-const member function), though it reads nothing from `this`. Unchanged across all versions.

functions.name: pointInTriangle
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::pointInTriangle(double ax, double ay, double bx, double by, double cx, double cy, double px, double py) const
functions.notes: Three cross products, in this exact order: (C,A), then (A,B), then (B,C) — i.e. term k is (next-p) x (cur-p) written as (Xnext-px)*(Ycur-py) - (Xcur-px)*(Ynext-py) with the pairs cycled C->A, A->B, B->C. All three compare `>= 0` (boundary counts as inside). Short-circuit && means later products are not even evaluated if an earlier one fails — irrelevant for the result but relevant if you were counting FLOPs. SIGN CONVENTION: this returns true for a triangle wound the way earcut expects an ear to be wound, i.e. one whose area(a,b,c) is NEGATIVE. Callers always pass (ear->prev, ear, ear->next) as (a,b,c) after already rejecting reflex ears, so the convention is self-consistent. VARIANT: earcut.js 3.0 (2024) rewrote this as three product-vs-product comparisons without the subtraction — `(cx-px)*(ay-py) >= (ax-px)*(cy-py) && (ax-px)*(by-py) >= (bx-px)*(ay-py) && (bx-px)*(cy-py) >= (cx-px)*(by-py)` — and added a companion `pointInTriangleExceptFirst(...)` = `!(ax==px && ay==py) && pointInTriangle(...)` used by isEar/isEarHashed. The C++ port at 2.2.4 does NOT have either of those; it keeps the subtracted `>= 0` form and has no ExceptFirst helper. The subtracted form and the product-comparison form are NOT bit-identical in floating point (the subtraction rounds once more), so pick the subtracted form for a 2.2.4-faithful port.

functions.name: sign
functions.signature: int Earcut<N>::sign(double val)
functions.notes: Written exactly as the difference of two bool-to-int conversions, with the comparisons in that order: (0.0 < val) minus (val < 0.0). Returns 1 / -1 / 0. NaN yields 0 - 0 = 0. The JS equivalent is `num > 0 ? 1 : num < 0 ? -1 : 0`, same result. Introduced together with the orientation-based `intersects` (earcut.js 2.2.0 / earcut.hpp 2.2.0); it does not exist in 2.1.x and earlier.

functions.name: onSegment
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::onSegment(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r)
functions.notes: Bounding-box containment of the MIDDLE argument q inside the box of p and r. Order of the four clauses: x<=max, x>=min, y<=max, y>=min — all inclusive. The explicit `std::max<double>` / `std::min<double>` template argument is in the real source (needed because the operands are already double; it is cosmetic). Only meaningful when the three points are collinear; callers guarantee that. New in 2.2.0.

functions.name: intersects (current, orientation-based, 2.2.x)
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::intersects(const Node* p1, const Node* q1, const Node* p2, const Node* q2)

functions.name: intersectsPolygon
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::intersectsPolygon(const Node* a, const Node* b)
functions.notes: Traversal starts AT a and walks forward via ->next until it returns to a (do/while, so edge (a, a->next) is the first edge examined and is then skipped by the guard). The guard compares INDICES (->i), not pointers — this matters because splitPolygon duplicates nodes with the same i, so a duplicate vertex node is also excluded. Guard clause order is exactly: p->i != a->i, then p->next->i != a->i, then p->i != b->i, then p->next->i != b->i, then the intersects() call; all joined by && so intersects() is only called for edges disjoint (by index) from both diagonal endpoints. Returns on the FIRST hit, so the traversal order is observable only through cost, not result. Unchanged in structure across versions; only the callee `intersects` changed.

functions.name: locallyInside
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::locallyInside(const Node* a, const Node* b)
functions.notes: Branch selector is `area(a->prev, a, a->next) < 0`, i.e. 'a is a CONVEX vertex' under earcut's negated sign convention. Convex branch: BOTH `area(a, b, a->next) >= 0` AND `area(a, a->prev, b) >= 0` (note >= , inclusive, and note the middle/last operand order differs between the two: (a,b,a->next) vs (a,a->prev,b)). Reflex branch: `area(a, b, a->prev) < 0` OR `area(a, a->next, b) < 0` (strict <, and again the operand orders are (a,b,a->prev) and (a,a->next,b)). The asymmetry >= vs < between branches is deliberate and load-bearing for degenerate/collinear inputs — do not 'normalize' it. Short-circuit matters only for cost. Identical in all versions 2.0.x–2.2.4 and in earcut.js 3.0.

functions.name: middleInside
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::middleInside(const Node* a, const Node* b)
functions.notes: Midpoint computed as (a->x + b->x) / 2 and (a->y + b->y) / 2 — sum then divide by 2, NOT 0.5*(...) (bit-identical here, but keep the form). Classic crossing-number ray cast to the LEFT-of-px test using strict `<`. Three conditions ANDed in this exact order: (1) `(p->y > py) != (p->next->y > py)` — strict > on both sides, so a vertex exactly at py counts as 'below'; (2) `p->next->y != p->y` — a guard added in 2.2.0 to avoid a 0/0 division producing NaN; it is logically implied by (1) for finite values but is present in the source and short-circuits BEFORE the division, so it changes floating-point/NaN behavior; (3) `px < (p->next->x - p->x) * (py - p->y) / (p->next->y - p->y) + p->x` — multiply first, then divide, then add p->x; do not refactor into a different association. Toggles `inside` on each crossing. Loop starts at a, walks ->next, do/while until back at a. Result is order-independent in exact arithmetic but NOT in floating point if you reorder the ring walk, so keep the start-at-a forward walk. OLDER VARIANT (2.1.x and earlier): identical except the `p->next->y != p->y` clause is absent.

functions.name: isValidDiagonal
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::isValidDiagonal(Node* a, Node* b)
functions.notes:
Exact top-level shape: A && B && C && (D || E), where the C++ source relies on && binding tighter than || (the extra parentheses above are for clarity; the original writes `... && !intersectsPolygon(a, b) && (locallyInside(a,b) && locallyInside(b,a) && middleInside(a,b) && (area(...) || area(...)) || equals(a,b) && area(...) > 0 && area(...) > 0)` with a single outer paren pair). Evaluation order left-to-right with short-circuiting; that order is observable via cost only.

Clause by clause:
- `a->next->i != b->i && a->prev->i != b->i` — index comparison, not pointer; b must not be an immediate neighbour of a.
- `!intersectsPolygon(a, b)`.
- opposite-facing-sectors clause: `(area(a->prev, a, b->prev) != 0 || area(a, b->prev, b) != 0)`. In C++ this is written with explicit `!= 0`; the JS writes the doubles as truthiness `(area(a.prev, a, b.prev) || area(a, b.prev, b))`. Same semantics except for NaN (NaN != 0 is true in C++, NaN is falsy in JS) — a real, if exotic, divergence.
- zero-length special case: `equals(a, b) && area(a->prev, a, a->next) > 0 && area(b->prev, b, b->next) > 0`. Note `> 0` (strictly positive = REFLEX under earcut's negated sign convention) at BOTH a and b, and note it uses a->prev/a->next and b->prev/b->next respectively.

OLDER SIMPLER VARIANTS:
- earcut.hpp 2.1.x / earcut.js <= 2.1.5: `return a->next->i != b->i && a->prev->i != b->i && !intersectsPolygon(a, b) && locallyInside(a, b) && locallyInside(b, a) && middleInside(a, b);` — a flat 6-way AND, no sectors clause, no zero-length clause.
- Very early (earcut.js 1.x / earcut.hpp 0.9-ish): same flat form, sometimes with the middleInside call taking a separate 'tip' argument or omitted entirely in the hole-bridging path.
- earcut.js 3.0 (2024): identical to the 2.2.x form shown above (truthiness spelling for the sectors clause).

functions.name: sectorContainsSector (adjacent predicate, used by findHoleBridge)
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::sectorContainsSector(const Node* m, const Node* p)
functions.notes: Included because it lives in the same predicate block and is easy to get backwards. Note the asymmetric operand order: first triple is (m->prev, m, p->prev), second is (p->next, m, m->next) — m is the MIDDLE argument in both. Both strict `< 0`. Introduced in 2.2.0 (used to disambiguate hole bridges at coincident x); absent in 2.1.x and earlier.

functions.name: filterPoints
functions.signature: typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::filterPoints(Node* start, Node* end = nullptr)
functions.notes:
Default argument `end = nullptr` is declared in the class body, not on the definition. Semantics point by point:
- `if (!end) end = start;` — the sentinel defaults to the start node.
- Removal test order: `!p->steiner` FIRST (steiner points are never filtered, even if duplicate/collinear), then `equals(p, p->next)` (duplicate of the FOLLOWING node, not the previous), then `area(p->prev, p, p->next) == 0` (exact zero, collinear).
- On removal: `removeNode(p); p = end = p->prev;` — BOTH the cursor and the sentinel move back to the predecessor. This is what lets the loop re-examine the predecessor (which may now itself be collinear) and guarantees the returned node is still linked.
- `if (p == p->next) break;` — the ring has collapsed to a single self-linked node; bail out immediately WITHOUT setting again. The function still returns `end`, which is that degenerate self-loop node — callers must tolerate it (earcutLinked's `if (!ear) return;` does not catch this; the ear loop's `ear->prev != ear->next` check does).
- `again = true;` after a successful removal forces at least one more iteration regardless of where p landed relative to end.
- Loop condition `while (again || p != end)` — `again` is checked first.
- Returns `end`: the last node that survived a removal, or the original start/end sentinel if nothing was removed. Callers reassign their ring handle from the return value (e.g. `ear = filterPoints(ear);`, `outerNode = filterPoints(outerNode, ...)`), so getting the return right is essential for downstream traversal start points and therefore for triangle emission order.
- earcut.js has an extra leading `if (!start) return start;`; the C++ header omits it (callers never pass null). If you want to be safe in a port, adding it is behavior-preserving for all reachable call sites.
- Unchanged across 2.0.x–2.2.4 and earcut.js 3.0. Very old (1.x) versions had a different signature/loop and no steiner flag.

functions.name: insertNode
functions.signature: template <typename Point> typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::insertNode(std::size_t i, const Point& pt, Node* last)
functions.notes: Inserts the new node immediately AFTER `last` (i.e. between last and last->next), and returns the NEW node — so linkedList's `last = insertNode(...)` walk builds the ring in input order and leaves `last` at the final vertex. With last == nullptr the node becomes a self-loop (prev = next = itself). Pointer assignment order in the non-null branch is exactly: p->next, p->prev, last->next->prev, last->next — the third statement must read last->next BEFORE the fourth overwrites it. z, prevZ, nextZ, steiner are left at their default-member-initializer values (0, nullptr, nullptr, false). The index is cast to N (narrowing from size_t) at construction.

functions.name: removeNode
functions.signature: void Earcut<N>::removeNode(Node* p)
functions.notes: Unlinks from BOTH doubly-linked lists: the polygon ring (prev/next) and the z-order list (prevZ/nextZ). Statement order: ring first (next->prev, then prev->next), then the two z-guards in the order prevZ, then nextZ. Each z unlink is guarded by a null check because the z list is a plain (non-circular) doubly-linked list with null ends, and because prevZ/nextZ are null entirely when hashing is off (indexCurve never ran). CRITICAL: removeNode does NOT clear p->prev, p->next, p->prevZ, or p->nextZ, and does NOT free the node — the removed node keeps dangling-but-valid pointers into the ring, and earcut relies on this (e.g. splitEarcut/cureLocalIntersections and the isEarHashed z-walk can still touch a node after it was removed). Do not add cleanup. The node stays alive in the ObjectPool until the pool is reset.

functions.name: splitPolygon (list surgery, included for completeness)
functions.signature: typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::splitPolygon(Node* a, Node* b)
functions.notes: Creates TWO duplicate nodes a2 (copy of a) and b2 (copy of b) — constructed in that order, a2 first — carrying the SAME index i as their originals. This is why every neighbour/exclusion test in this subsystem compares ->i rather than pointers. `an` and `bp` are captured BEFORE any relinking. Eight pointer writes in exactly the order shown. Returns b2 (the copy of b in the second/new ring). The new nodes get z=0, prevZ=nextZ=nullptr, steiner=false, so a split ring is not in the z-index — callers that were hashing must re-run indexCurve on the pieces (earcutLinked does, via its pass logic).

input.determinismNotes:
Things that must be preserved byte-for-byte to reproduce identical triangle output:

1. area() expression form: `(q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`. Any algebraic rearrangement (e.g. the more common (b-a)x(c-a) form) changes both the sign convention and the last-bit rounding, and area()==0 / area()>0 tests appear in filterPoints, isValidDiagonal, locallyInside, isEar and the hole-bridge code, so a 1-ulp difference flips triangulations on collinear-ish data.

2. Sign convention is inverted relative to the usual math convention: negative area == convex/CCW. Every `< 0` / `>= 0` / `> 0` in locallyInside, isValidDiagonal, sectorContainsSector, isEar depends on it.

3. pointInTriangle's three products are the SUBTRACTED form compared `>= 0` (2.2.4), not the product-vs-product form of earcut.js 3.0. The two round differently.

4. All coordinates are promoted to double at linkedList time; do not do predicate arithmetic in the input scalar type (e.g. float or int), and do not use long double or FMA. Compile without -ffast-math and without x87 excess precision (-mfpmath=sse on 32-bit x86, or the equivalent), otherwise the exact-zero tests (`area(...) == 0`, `sign()`) misbehave.

5. Traversal directions: intersectsPolygon and middleInside both start AT `a` and walk FORWARD via ->next in a do/while. filterPoints walks forward but rewinds to ->prev on every removal. Reversing any of these changes floating-point accumulation (middleInside) or which edge is found first (intersectsPolygon, cost only) and, for filterPoints, changes the returned node and therefore the start vertex of every downstream loop — which directly reorders emitted triangles.

6. filterPoints' return value IS part of the algorithm's state, not a convenience. `end` advances backwards on removals. Callers assign it back to the ring handle.

7. Index (->i) comparisons, never pointer comparisons, in intersectsPolygon and isValidDiagonal — because splitPolygon manufactures duplicate nodes sharing an index.

8. removeNode leaves the removed node's own pointers intact; other code depends on reading through them afterwards.

9. Short-circuit order in isValidDiagonal and locallyInside affects only cost, not the result — except in the presence of NaN, where the C++ `!= 0` spelling of the sectors clause differs from the JS truthiness spelling.

10. equals() is exact ==; there is no epsilon anywhere in earcut.

uncertainties.what: Whether earcut.hpp 2.2.4's pointInTriangle uses the subtracted `>= 0` form or the product-vs-product `>=` form.
uncertainties.alternatives: (a) `(cx-px)*(ay-py) - (ax-px)*(cy-py) >= 0 && ...` (what I reported); (b) `(cx-px)*(ay-py) >= (ax-px)*(cy-py) && ...` as in earcut.js 3.0. If the C++ header was refreshed from JS 3.0 after Aug 2022, (b) would apply, and a `pointInTriangleExceptFirst` helper would also exist and be called from isEar/isEarHashed with the ear's own prev/next. These two forms differ in last-bit rounding and thus can differ in output on degenerate data.
uncertainties.confidence: ~85% that the released 2.2.4 header uses form (a) with no ExceptFirst helper. If your reference build is 'latest master' rather than the 2.2.4 tag, verify this one function first — it is the single most likely divergence in this subsystem.

uncertainties.what: Presence of a leading `if (!start) return start;` in the C++ filterPoints.
uncertainties.alternatives: earcut.js definitely has it. I believe the C++ header omits it and only has `if (!end) end = start;`. Adding it is behavior-preserving for all in-tree call sites, so this cannot change output — only crash behavior on a null argument.
uncertainties.confidence: ~70% that C++ omits it; zero impact on emitted triangles either way.

uncertainties.what: Exact spelling of the min/max calls in onSegment.
uncertainties.alternatives: `std::max<double>(p->x, r->x)` (explicit template arg, what I reported) vs plain `std::max(p->x, r->x)`. Purely cosmetic — both compile to the same comparison, and both are IEEE-identical for non-NaN doubles.
uncertainties.confidence: ~75% on the explicit <double>; no semantic impact.

uncertainties.what: Whether the older (pre-2.2) `intersects` guard used `(equals(p1,q1) && equals(p2,q2)) || (equals(p1,q2) && equals(p2,q1))` exactly in that clause order.
uncertainties.alternatives: The pairing could conceivably have been written with the operands swapped. The predicate is symmetric so the result is identical; only source appearance differs.
uncertainties.confidence: ~90% on the clause content; the clause ORDER has no observable effect.

input.determinismNotes:
Things that must be preserved byte-for-byte to reproduce identical triangle output:

1. area() expression form: `(q->y - p->y) * (r->x - q->x) - (q->x - p->x) * (r->y - q->y)`. Any algebraic rearrangement (e.g. the more common (b-a)x(c-a) form) changes both the sign convention and the last-bit rounding, and area()==0 / area()>0 tests appear in filterPoints, isValidDiagonal, locallyInside, isEar and the hole-bridge code, so a 1-ulp difference flips triangulations on collinear-ish data.

2. Sign convention is inverted relative to the usual math convention: negative area == convex/CCW. Every `< 0` / `>= 0` / `> 0` in locallyInside, isValidDiagonal, sectorContainsSector, isEar depends on it.

3. pointInTriangle's three products are the SUBTRACTED form compared `>= 0` (2.2.4), not the product-vs-product form of earcut.js 3.0. The two round differently.

4. All coordinates are promoted to double at linkedList time; do not do predicate arithmetic in the input scalar type (e.g. float or int), and do not use long double or FMA. Compile without -ffast-math and without x87 excess precision (-mfpmath=sse on 32-bit x86, or the equivalent), otherwise the exact-zero tests (`area(...) == 0`, `sign()`) misbehave.

5. Traversal directions: intersectsPolygon and middleInside both start AT `a` and walk FORWARD via ->next in a do/while. filterPoints walks forward but rewinds to ->prev on every removal. Reversing any of these changes floating-point accumulation (middleInside) or which edge is found first (intersectsPolygon, cost only) and, for filterPoints, changes the returned node and therefore the start vertex of every downstream loop — which directly reorders emitted triangles.

6. filterPoints' return value IS part of the algorithm's state, not a convenience. `end` advances backwards on removals. Callers assign it back to the ring handle.

7. Index (->i) comparisons, never pointer comparisons, in intersectsPolygon and isValidDiagonal — because splitPolygon manufactures duplicate nodes sharing an index.

8. removeNode leaves the removed node's own pointers intact; other code depends on reading through them afterwards.

9. Short-circuit order in isValidDiagonal and locallyInside affects only cost, not the result — except in the presence of NaN, where the C++ `!= 0` spelling of the sectors clause differs from the JS truthiness spelling.

10. equals() is exact ==; there is no epsilon anywhere in earcut.

functions.name: Node (struct, for reference — field order matters for the surgery routines)
functions.notes: x and y are ALWAYS double, regardless of the coordinate type of the input points (linkedList does util::nth<0,Point>::get(pt) into a double). So all predicate arithmetic is IEEE-754 double even for integer input. `i` is of the output index type N (e.g. uint32_t). Nodes are allocated from an ObjectPool<Node> member named `nodes`; pool identity/addresses are never compared for ordering, only for equality, so allocator behavior does not affect output.
functions.signature: struct Node { Node(N index, double x_, double y_); const N i; const double x; const double y; Node* prev = nullptr; Node* next = nullptr; int32_t z = 0; Node* prevZ = nullptr; Node* nextZ = nullptr; bool steiner = false; };

functions.name: area
functions.notes: DO NOT rearrange. Exactly: (q.y-p.y)*(r.x-q.x) - (q.x-p.x)*(r.y-q.y). Sign convention: this is the NEGATIVE of the usual CCW cross product. For p=(0,0), q=(1,0), r=(0,1) (counter-clockwise in standard math orientation) it returns -1. Hence in earcut a NEGATIVE area means convex/CCW turn, and `area(...) >= 0` means reflex. This is why isEar starts with `if (area(a,b,c) >= 0) return false; // reflex, can't be an ear`, and why signedArea/linkedList orient the outer ring so that traversal yields negative areas. This form and sign convention are IDENTICAL in every version from 0.x through 2.2.4 and in earcut.js 3.0.
functions.signature: double Earcut<N>::area(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r) const

functions.name: equals
functions.notes: Exact double equality (==), both coordinates, x tested first with short-circuit &&. No epsilon anywhere in earcut. It is a plain non-const member function in the header (not marked const), though it reads nothing from `this`. Unchanged across all versions.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::equals(const Node* p1, const Node* p2)

functions.name: pointInTriangle
functions.notes: Three cross products, in this exact order: the (C,A) pair, then (A,B), then (B,C) — i.e. the pairs are cycled C->A, A->B, B->C, and each term is written (Xfirst-px)*(Ysecond-py) - (Xsecond-px)*(Yfirst-py). All three compare `>= 0` (boundary counts as inside). Short-circuit && means later products are not evaluated if an earlier one fails — irrelevant to the result. SIGN CONVENTION: this returns true for a triangle wound the way earcut expects an ear to be wound, i.e. one whose area(a,b,c) is NEGATIVE. Callers always pass (ear->prev, ear, ear->next) as (a,b,c) after already rejecting reflex ears, so the convention is self-consistent. Sanity check: a=(0,0), b=(1,0), c=(0,1) (area = -1) with p=(0.2,0.2) yields +0.2, +0.2, +0.6 — all >= 0, inside. VARIANT: earcut.js 3.0 (2024) rewrote this as three product-vs-product comparisons without the subtraction — `(cx-px)*(ay-py) >= (ax-px)*(cy-py) && (ax-px)*(by-py) >= (bx-px)*(ay-py) && (bx-px)*(cy-py) >= (cx-px)*(by-py)` — and added a companion `pointInTriangleExceptFirst(...)` = `!(ax==px && ay==py) && pointInTriangle(...)` used by isEar/isEarHashed. The C++ port at 2.2.4 has NEITHER; it keeps the subtracted `>= 0` form and has no ExceptFirst helper. The subtracted and product-comparison forms are NOT bit-identical (the subtraction rounds once more), so use the subtracted form for a 2.2.4-faithful port.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::pointInTriangle(double ax, double ay, double bx, double by, double cx, double cy, double px, double py) const

functions.name: sign
functions.notes: Written exactly as the difference of two bool-to-int conversions, with the comparisons in that order: (0.0 < val) minus (val < 0.0). Returns 1 / -1 / 0. NaN yields 0 - 0 = 0. The JS equivalent is `num > 0 ? 1 : num < 0 ? -1 : 0`, same result. Introduced together with the orientation-based `intersects` (earcut.js 2.2.0 / earcut.hpp 2.2.0); it does not exist in 2.1.x and earlier.
functions.signature: int Earcut<N>::sign(double val)

functions.name: onSegment
functions.notes: Bounding-box containment of the MIDDLE argument q inside the box of p and r. Order of the four clauses: x<=max, x>=min, y<=max, y>=min — all inclusive. The explicit `std::max<double>` / `std::min<double>` template argument is in the real source (operands are already double, so it is cosmetic). Only meaningful when the three points are collinear; callers guarantee that. New in 2.2.0.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::onSegment(const Node* p, const Node* q, const Node* r)

functions.name: intersects (current orientation-based version, 2.2.x)
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::intersects(const Node* p1, const Node* q1, const Node* p2, const Node* q2)

functions.name: intersectsPolygon
functions.notes: Traversal starts AT a and walks forward via ->next until it returns to a (do/while, so edge (a, a->next) is the first edge examined and is then skipped by the guard). The guard compares INDICES (->i), not pointers — this matters because splitPolygon duplicates nodes with the same i, so a duplicate vertex node is also excluded. Guard clause order is exactly: p->i != a->i, then p->next->i != a->i, then p->i != b->i, then p->next->i != b->i, then the intersects() call; all joined by && so intersects() is only invoked for edges disjoint (by index) from both diagonal endpoints. Returns on the FIRST hit, so traversal order is observable only through cost, not result. Structure unchanged across versions; only the callee `intersects` changed.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::intersectsPolygon(const Node* a, const Node* b)

functions.name: locallyInside
functions.notes: Branch selector is `area(a->prev, a, a->next) < 0`, i.e. 'a is a CONVEX vertex' under earcut's negated sign convention. Convex branch: BOTH `area(a, b, a->next) >= 0` AND `area(a, a->prev, b) >= 0` — note `>=` (inclusive) and note the operand orders differ between the two calls: (a, b, a->next) vs (a, a->prev, b). Reflex branch: `area(a, b, a->prev) < 0` OR `area(a, a->next, b) < 0` — strict `<`, operand orders (a, b, a->prev) and (a, a->next, b). The asymmetry (>= in the convex branch, < in the reflex branch) is deliberate and load-bearing for degenerate/collinear inputs; do not 'normalize' it. Short-circuit affects cost only. Identical in all versions 2.0.x–2.2.4 and in earcut.js 3.0.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::locallyInside(const Node* a, const Node* b)

functions.name: middleInside
functions.notes: Midpoint computed as (a->x + b->x) / 2 and (a->y + b->y) / 2 — sum then divide by 2, NOT 0.5*(...) (bit-identical here, but keep the form). Classic crossing-number ray cast using strict `<`. Three conditions ANDed in exactly this order: (1) `(p->y > py) != (p->next->y > py)` — strict `>` on both sides, so a vertex exactly at py counts as 'below'; (2) `p->next->y != p->y` — guard added in 2.2.0 to avoid a 0/0 division producing NaN; logically implied by (1) for finite values but present in the source and short-circuiting BEFORE the division, so it changes NaN behavior; (3) `px < (p->next->x - p->x) * (py - p->y) / (p->next->y - p->y) + p->x` — multiply first, then divide, then add p->x; do not re-associate. Toggles `inside` on each crossing. Loop starts at a, walks ->next, do/while until back at a. The result is order-independent in exact arithmetic but not necessarily in floating point, so keep the start-at-a forward walk. OLDER VARIANT (2.1.x and earlier): identical except the `p->next->y != p->y` clause is absent.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::middleInside(const Node* a, const Node* b)

functions.name: isValidDiagonal
functions.notes:
Exact top-level shape: A && B && C && (D || E). The original source relies on && binding tighter than ||, writing a single outer paren pair: `... && !intersectsPolygon(a, b) && (locallyInside(a,b) && locallyInside(b,a) && middleInside(a,b) && (area(...) != 0 || area(...) != 0) || equals(a,b) && area(...) > 0 && area(...) > 0)`. The extra parens in my pseudocode are only for clarity and do not change grouping. Evaluation is left-to-right with short-circuiting; that order is observable via cost only.

Clause by clause:
- `a->next->i != b->i && a->prev->i != b->i` — index comparison, not pointer; b must not be an immediate neighbour of a.
- `!intersectsPolygon(a, b)`.
- locally visible: `locallyInside(a, b) && locallyInside(b, a) && middleInside(a, b)` in that order.
- opposite-facing-sectors clause: `(area(a->prev, a, b->prev) != 0 || area(a, b->prev, b) != 0)`. Note the operand triples: (a->prev, a, b->prev) and (a, b->prev, b) — both involve b->prev, neither involves b->next. C++ writes explicit `!= 0`; earcut.js writes the doubles as truthiness `(area(a.prev, a, b.prev) || area(a, b.prev, b))`. Same semantics except for NaN (NaN != 0 is true in C++, NaN is falsy in JS) — a real if exotic divergence.
- zero-length special case: `equals(a, b) && area(a->prev, a, a->next) > 0 && area(b->prev, b, b->next) > 0`. Note `> 0` (strictly positive = REFLEX under earcut's negated sign convention) at BOTH a and b, using a's own prev/next and b's own prev/next respectively.

OLDER SIMPLER VARIANTS:
- earcut.hpp 2.1.x / earcut.js <= 2.1.5: a flat 6-way AND with no sectors clause and no zero-length clause — `return a->next->i != b->i && a->prev->i != b->i && !intersectsPolygon(a, b) && locallyInside(a, b) && locallyInside(b, a) && middleInside(a, b);`
- Very early (earcut.js 1.x / earcut.hpp 0.9-era): same flat form, with middleInside sometimes taking a separate 'tip' argument or being omitted on the hole-bridging path.
- earcut.js 3.0 (2024): identical to the 2.2.x form above (truthiness spelling for the sectors clause).
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::isValidDiagonal(Node* a, Node* b)

functions.name: sectorContainsSector (adjacent predicate, used by findHoleBridge)
functions.notes: Included because it lives in the same predicate block and is easy to get backwards. Note the asymmetric operand order: the first triple is (m->prev, m, p->prev), the second is (p->next, m, m->next) — m is the MIDDLE argument in both. Both strict `< 0`, joined by &&. Introduced in 2.2.0 to disambiguate hole bridges at coincident x; absent in 2.1.x and earlier.
functions.signature: bool Earcut<N>::sectorContainsSector(const Node* m, const Node* p)

functions.name: filterPoints
functions.notes:
The default argument `end = nullptr` is declared in the class body, not on the out-of-line definition. Semantics point by point:
- `if (!end) end = start;` — the sentinel defaults to the start node.
- Removal test order: `!p->steiner` FIRST (steiner points are never filtered, even if duplicate or collinear), then `equals(p, p->next)` (duplicate of the FOLLOWING node, not the previous), then `area(p->prev, p, p->next) == 0` (exact zero = collinear).
- On removal: `removeNode(p); p = end = p->prev;` — BOTH the cursor and the sentinel move back to the predecessor. This is what lets the loop re-examine the predecessor (which may itself now be collinear) and guarantees the returned node is still linked. Note p->prev is read from the removed node, which removeNode deliberately leaves intact.
- `if (p == p->next) break;` — the ring has collapsed to a single self-linked node; bail out immediately WITHOUT setting `again`. The function still returns `end`, which is that degenerate self-loop node, so callers must tolerate it (earcutLinked's `if (!ear) return;` does not catch it; the ear loop's `ear->prev != ear->next` check does).
- `again = true;` after a successful removal forces at least one more iteration regardless of where p landed relative to end.
- Loop condition `while (again || p != end)` — `again` is checked first.
- RETURNS `end`: the last node that survived a removal, or the original start/end sentinel if nothing was removed. Callers reassign their ring handle from the return value (`ear = filterPoints(ear);`, `outerNode = filterPoints(outerNode, ...)`), so the return value determines downstream traversal start points and therefore triangle emission order.
- earcut.js has an extra leading `if (!start) return start;`; the C++ header omits it (callers never pass null). Adding it is behavior-preserving for all reachable call sites.
- Unchanged across 2.0.x–2.2.4 and earcut.js 3.0. Very old (1.x) versions had a different signature/loop and no steiner flag.
functions.signature: typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::filterPoints(Node* start, Node* end = nullptr)

functions.name: insertNode
functions.notes: Inserts the new node immediately AFTER `last` (between last and last->next) and returns the NEW node — so linkedList's `last = insertNode(...)` walk builds the ring in input order and leaves `last` at the final vertex. With last == nullptr the node becomes a self-loop (prev = next = itself). Pointer assignment order in the non-null branch is exactly: p->next, p->prev, last->next->prev, last->next — the third statement must read last->next BEFORE the fourth overwrites it. z, prevZ, nextZ, steiner keep their default-member-initializer values (0, nullptr, nullptr, false). The index is narrowed to N via static_cast at construction.
functions.signature: template <typename Point> typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::insertNode(std::size_t i, const Point& pt, Node* last)

functions.name: removeNode
functions.notes: Unlinks from BOTH doubly-linked lists: the polygon ring (prev/next) and the z-order list (prevZ/nextZ). Statement order: ring first (p->next->prev = p->prev, then p->prev->next = p->next), then the two z-guards in the order prevZ, then nextZ. Each z unlink is guarded by a null check because the z list is a plain non-circular doubly-linked list with null ends, and because prevZ/nextZ are null entirely when hashing is off (indexCurve never ran). CRITICAL: removeNode does NOT clear p->prev, p->next, p->prevZ or p->nextZ, and does NOT free the node — the removed node keeps dangling-but-valid pointers into the ring and earcut relies on this (filterPoints reads p->prev right after removing p; cureLocalIntersections/splitEarcut and the isEarHashed z-walk can also still touch removed nodes). Do not add cleanup. The node stays alive in the ObjectPool until the pool is reset.
functions.signature: void Earcut<N>::removeNode(Node* p)

functions.name: splitPolygon (list surgery, included for completeness)
functions.notes: Creates TWO duplicate nodes: a2 (copy of a) and b2 (copy of b), constructed in that order, a2 first, each carrying the SAME index i as its original. This is precisely why every neighbour/exclusion test in this subsystem compares ->i rather than pointers. `an = a->next` and `bp = b->prev` are captured BEFORE any relinking. Eight pointer writes in exactly the order shown. Returns b2 (the copy of b that lands in the second/new ring). The new nodes get z=0, prevZ=nextZ=nullptr, steiner=false, so a split ring is not in the z-index and callers that were hashing must re-run indexCurve on the pieces (earcutLinked does, via its pass logic).
functions.signature: typename Earcut<N>::Node* Earcut<N>::splitPolygon(Node* a, Node* b)
